meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'God helps those who help themselves'?
meta.ogDescription: Not in the Bible at all. The exact wording first appears in Algernon Sidney (1698); Franklin's Poor Richard made it famous. The sentiment is an old Greek proverb.

answer.label: Not the Bible — first penned by Algernon Sidney
answer.sourceLine: This is the single most famous line people believe is in the Bible — and it is not scripture at all. The exact modern wording first appears in Algernon Sidney’s Discourses Concerning Government (published 1698, ch. 2 §23), and Benjamin Franklin fixed it in American memory in Poor Richard’s Almanack (1736), where he printed the variant “God helps them that help themselves.” The sentiment itself is an ancient Greek proverb, older than either man.

source.heading: Where the words actually come from

docMeta.dd: No — it appears in no book of scripture

source.excerpt: God helps those who help themselves.
trail: An ancient Greek proverb underlies it — Aesop’s Hercules and the Wagoner ends “the gods help them that help themselves,” and Euripides and Sophocles voice the same idea centuries before Christ.
The exact modern wording first appears in Algernon Sidney’s Discourses Concerning Government, quoted at Wikiquote as “God helps those who help themselves” (ch. 2 §23).
Benjamin Franklin printed the near-identical “God helps them that help themselves” in Poor Richard’s Almanack (1736), cementing it in American speech — but he did not coin it.
It is not in the Bible, yet polls have found roughly three in four Americans believe it is scripture.
source.excerptNote: The wording is the tail end of a long lineage. Euripides had “Try first thyself, and after call in God”; Aesop’s wagoner is told “the gods help them that help themselves”; George Herbert’s Jacula Prudentum (1651) gives “Help thyself, and God will help thee.” Sidney supplied the exact phrasing we quote today.

author.heading: Who really wrote it
author.metaLine: 1623–1683 · English politician & political theorist; author of Discourses Concerning Government
author.bio: Algernon Sidney was an English republican politician and political theorist whose Discourses Concerning Government argued against absolute monarchy and the divine right of kings. Written in reply to Robert Filmer, the manuscript was used as evidence to convict Sidney of treason, and he was executed in 1683; the work was published posthumously in 1698 and later influenced the American revolutionaries. It is in that book that the exact wording “God helps those who help themselves” first appears in English.

misattribution.heading: Why everyone thinks it's in the Bible
misattribution.intro: This is the textbook case of a secular proverb mistaken for scripture. It is quotable, moralizing, and God-mentioning — so it gets filed under “the Bible” by default.

items.why: The line appears in no book of the Bible in any translation. Surveys have repeatedly found a large majority of Americans — in some polls around 75–82% — believe it is a Bible verse, and it has even topped lists of “best-known Bible verses.” Many theologians note it actually runs counter to scripture’s emphasis on grace and dependence on God.

Franklin printed “God helps them that help themselves” in Poor Richard’s Almanack (1736) and made it an American byword, but he was collecting proverbs, not coining them — the exact modern wording already existed in Sidney’s 1698 Discourses.

misattribution.truthLine: The exact wording first appears in Algernon Sidney’s Discourses Concerning Government (1698); the sentiment is an ancient Greek proverb — and it is not in the Bible.

context.heading: Why the line matters
lead: Few sayings reveal the gap between folk belief and text like this one. It has become a small article of secular faith — a self-reliance creed dressed in religious language — which is exactly why so many assume a chapter and verse must exist for it.

Its real history is a chain of borrowing: an ancient Greek proverb voiced by Euripides and Aesop, condensed by George Herbert, given its exact English shape by a 17th-century republican on trial for his life, and finally broadcast to a nation by a printer selling almanacs.
context.pull: The most-quoted “Bible verse” that is not in the Bible.
